fixes.explanation: True. Ezra 1:7 says Nebuchadnezzar had carried the articles away from Jerusalem and "placed in the temple of his gods." Now King Cyrus is bringing them out. Good eye, baker.
It's true, friend. Ezra 1:7 says Nebuchadnezzar had carried the articles away from Jerusalem and "placed in the temple of his gods." Then King Cyrus brought them out.

Ezra 1:1 says the LORD stirred Cyrus's spirit "…to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah…" The LORD had said it, and now He was making it happen. Cyrus, king of Persia, is the one who gets stirred, and then he puts a proclamation in writing for his whole kingdom. That's a king who doesn't lose the memo.

Nice thinking, but the verse doesn't say that. It gives one reason: the LORD stirred Cyrus's spirit "…to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah…" (Ezra 1:1). Repaying isn't mentioned anywhere in it, friend, so nobody's handing out a refund receipt here.

Yes, a house. Cyrus says the LORD "…has appointed me to build a house for Him at Jerusalem in Judah." (Ezra 1:2). Cyrus, king of Persia, is the one saying it. A king with a whole kingdom to run, and he's announcing a house for the LORD, in writing, no less.

Wall is a good builder's guess, friend, but Cyrus doesn't say wall. He says the LORD "…has appointed me to build a house for Him at Jerusalem in Judah." (Ezra 1:2). The project on the table is a house for the LORD.

That's the one. Cyrus says, "…may his God be with him, and may he go to Jerusalem in Judah…" (Ezra 1:3). The wish is that God be with him. Cyrus is the king of Persia, and he's wishing it for people who belong to the LORD.

Ha, that's a king-sounding answer. But Cyrus wishes no such thing in the text. He says, "…may his God be with him, and may he go to Jerusalem in Judah…" (Ezra 1:3). His wish for them is that their God be with them.

That's him. Ezra 1:8 says Mithredath the treasurer "…counted them out to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah." Verse 11 says Sheshbazzar brought all these along when the exiles went up from Babylon to Jerusalem. That's 5,400 articles, friend, and I'd want that man on inventory day.
Yes. Ezra 2:62 says these men searched for their family records, couldn't find them, and "…so were excluded from the priesthood as unclean." Records mattered for priests. I think this one hurts.

True. Ezra 2:63 says, "The governor ordered them not to eat the most holy things until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim." So the matter waits until there's a priest to consult them. Good eye, baker.

It's true, friend. Ezra 2:63 says, "The governor ordered them not to eat the most holy things until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim." That's a governor's order, and it's right there in the text. Nobody's guessing on this one.

Yes. Ezra 2:68 says, "…some of the heads of the families gave freewill offerings to rebuild the house of God on its original site." Some of the heads of the families, that's who the verse names. You read that carefully, baker.
Right. Ezra 2:68 says they gave "…to rebuild the house of God on its original site." That means the old spot, not a new one. Same spot, friend. No moving the house across town.

Same amount is a fair thought, friend. Ezra 2:69 says, "According to their ability, they gave to the treasury for this work…" The measure the verse gives is ability, and no set amount per person is named.
